question: What is the Strategy pattern and what problem does it solve?
title: Strategy Pattern Explained
direct_answer: Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface, allowing clients to switch algorithms at runtime without modifying the context. It solves the problem of messy if-else chains and makes behavior changes easy by creating separate classes for each algorithm.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can identify the if-else anti-pattern and explain how Strategy eliminates it through polymorphism
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Strategy is just about using interfaces without explaining the specific problem of tightly coupled conditional logic it solves
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete before-and-after transformation where a 20-line if-else block becomes three clean strategy classes

sections.title: Strategy Pattern Fundamentals
sections.content: The **Strategy pattern** solves the problem of tightly coupled conditional logic that changes based on runtime conditions. Imagine a cart service that calculates discounts differently for premium members, seasonal sales, and bulk orders. Without Strategy, you'd have a massive if-else chain that grows every time marketing adds a new promotion type. **The core problem**: each new discount rule requires modifying the same method, violating the Open-Closed Principle and making testing painful. Strategy extracts each algorithm into its own class implementing a common interface. The cart service holds a reference to the **strategy interface**, not concrete implementations, and delegates the calculation. **Think of it like a restaurant**: the waiter (context) doesn't need to know how each dish is cooked (strategy), they just hand the order to the kitchen interface and serve what comes back. The key insight is **separating what varies from what stays the same** — the discount calculation logic varies, but the flow of applying a discount to a cart total remains constant.

sections.title: Discount Strategy Implementation
Key Points
content: **Strategy interface**: defines a common contract that all algorithm implementations must follow, enabling polymorphic behavior without the context knowing concrete types
**Concrete strategies**: each encapsulates one specific algorithm as a separate class, making it easy to add new strategies without touching existing code
**Context class**: holds a reference to the strategy interface and delegates algorithm execution, never containing if-else logic to pick strategies
**Open-Closed Principle**: you can add new strategies by creating new classes without modifying the context, keeping changes localized and safe
**Runtime flexibility**: strategies can be swapped at runtime by passing different implementations, unlike inheritance which locks behavior at compile time
**Testability**: each strategy can be unit tested in isolation, and the context can be tested with mock strategies injected via constructor
**if-else elimination**: replaces conditional branches with polymorphism, turning branching logic into class selection done outside the context

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Strategy pattern is about replacing if-else chains with separate classes that each implement one algorithm. The problem it solves is when you have code that does different things based on some condition, and that conditional logic keeps growing. For example, say you're building a cart service that calculates discounts. Without Strategy, you'd write something like if customer is premium then apply fifteen percent off, else if order is over a thousand then apply ten percent off, else no discount. Every time marketing adds a new promotion, you modify that same method. Strategy fixes this by creating a DiscountStrategy interface with an applyDiscount method, then you make separate classes like PremiumMemberDiscount and BulkOrderDiscount that implement it. The cart service gets the strategy through its constructor and just calls applyDiscount without knowing which one it has. The key thing interviewers want to hear is that the context class doesn't pick the strategy, it receives it from outside. This makes adding new discount types easy because you just create a new class, no existing code changes. A common mistake freshers make is putting the if-else inside the context to choose which strategy to use, but that defeats the whole purpose. You want to select the strategy externally, maybe in a factory or through dependency injection, and pass it in. This way your cart service is closed for modification but open for extension, which is exactly what the Open-Closed Principle means in practice.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Strategy pattern is the antidote to a specific smell — the if-else chain that grows every time you add a new behavior type.

beats.content: Imagine a checkout service: if payment type is CREDIT_CARD do this, else if UPI do that, else if COD do the other thing. Every new payment method means editing this method. That's an OCP violation — the class changes for every extension.

Strategy fixes it: define a PaymentStrategy interface with a single processPayment method. CreditCardStrategy, UPIStrategy, and CODStrategy each implement it with their own logic. PaymentService just holds a PaymentStrategy and calls it — no if-else, no knowledge of which type it got.

content: Context (PaymentService) delegates to strategy — doesn't choose the algorithm
Strategy is injected from outside — by the caller, a factory, or Spring DI
Adding a new payment method = new strategy class, zero changes to PaymentService

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: Java's Comparator is the canonical Strategy example. Collections.sort() is the context; the comparison algorithm is the strategy you inject. Lambdas make Strategy a one-liner.

question: How do you implement Strategy pattern for a payment system in Java?
title: Strategy Pattern: Payment System Implementation
direct_answer: Define a PaymentStrategy interface with a processPayment method, create concrete classes like CreditCardPayment, UPIPayment, and CODPayment that implement it, then inject the chosen strategy into PaymentService via constructor. The service calls processPayment without knowing which payment type it's executing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can implement the pattern with proper separation — strategy selection happens outside the context, not inside it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting the if-else that picks the strategy inside PaymentService's processPayment method, which just moves the problem instead of solving it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how the strategy is selected externally — either via a factory, Spring DI with qualifiers, or passed directly from the controller layer

sections.title: Payment Strategy Architecture
sections.content: A payment system is the **classic Strategy pattern use case** because payment methods vary widely in their processing logic — credit cards need validation and gateway calls, UPI requires QR generation and callback handling, cash on delivery just marks an order as pending. **The wrong approach** is a PaymentService with a giant switch statement on payment type that grows every time you add PayPal, wallet payments, or crypto. Strategy pattern splits each payment method into its own class implementing **PaymentStrategy interface**. The **PaymentService context** receives the strategy through dependency injection and delegates processing. **Critical design choice**: the service never contains logic to pick which strategy to use. That decision happens **upstream** — either the controller layer selects it based on request parameters, a factory builds it, or Spring injects it using qualifiers. This separation means adding Bitcoin payments doesn't require touching PaymentService at all, you just write a new BitcoinPayment class and wire it in. The pattern keeps payment processing logic isolated and testable.

sections.title: Payment Strategy with Spring DI
Key Points
content: **PaymentStrategy interface**: defines the contract with a processPayment method that all payment types must implement, ensuring consistent behavior across different methods
**Concrete strategy classes**: each encapsulates one payment method's complete logic including validation, API calls, and result handling, keeping them independent
**Context dependency injection**: PaymentService receives the strategy via constructor parameter, never instantiating it with new, which enables testing with mocks
**External strategy selection**: the choice of which payment method to use happens outside PaymentService, typically in the controller or a factory based on user input
**No conditional logic in context**: PaymentService contains zero if-else or switch statements for payment types, it just calls the injected strategy's method
**Spring component annotations**: marking each strategy with at-Component and a name enables Spring to manage them as beans and inject them where needed
**Qualifier-based wiring**: using at-Qualifier in the constructor tells Spring which specific implementation to inject when multiple PaymentStrategy beans exist

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To implement Strategy pattern for a payment system, you start by defining a PaymentStrategy interface with a processPayment method that takes the order and amount. Then you create concrete classes for each payment type, like CreditCardPayment, UPIPayment, and CODPayment, each implementing that interface with its own logic. The key part is the PaymentService context class receives the strategy through its constructor, not by creating it internally. In Spring, you'd annotate each payment class with at-Component and give it a name, then in PaymentService you'd use at-Autowired with at-Qualifier to inject the one you want. The service just calls processPayment on whatever strategy it got, it doesn't know or care which payment type it's using. That's the whole point of the pattern. Where freshers mess up is they put the if-else logic inside PaymentService to pick which strategy to use, like if payment type equals credit card then use this strategy. That defeats the purpose because you're still modifying the context every time you add a new payment method. The right way is to select the strategy outside the service. For example, in the controller you'd look at the request parameter, maybe the user selected UPI, then you'd inject or pass the UPI strategy to the service. Or you can use a factory that takes the payment type string and returns the right strategy. The benefit is when you add PayPal support, you just write a new PayPalPayment class and register it with Spring, you don't touch PaymentService at all. That's how Strategy keeps your code open for extension but closed for modification.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: The payment system example makes Strategy concrete — and showing the before vs after transformation is exactly what interviewers want to see.

beats.content: Define PaymentStrategy with one method: process(PaymentRequest). Write CreditCardPaymentStrategy, UPIPaymentStrategy, CODPaymentStrategy — each handles its own gateway logic.

PaymentService holds a Map from payment method to strategy. At checkout, a lookup replaces the if-else: strategy = strategies.get(paymentMethod), then strategy.process(request). No switch, no conditionals in the service itself.

In Spring, annotate each strategy with @Component. PaymentService gets a Map<String, PaymentStrategy> auto-injected — Spring collects all PaymentStrategy beans by bean name as the map key. Adding WalletPaymentStrategy means one new class — the map grows automatically, PaymentService is untouched.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: The strategy selection still has to happen somewhere. It moves to the caller or a factory — not to the context class. If PaymentService still has an if-else to choose which strategy to use, you've only moved the problem, not solved it.

question: How does Java's Comparator demonstrate the Strategy pattern?
title: Comparator as Strategy Pattern in Java
direct_answer: Comparator is a strategy for comparing objects. Collections.sort and List.sort are the context classes that accept any Comparator implementation without knowing its internal logic. You pass different comparison algorithms to the same sort method, demonstrating runtime strategy selection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can recognize Strategy pattern in real-world Java APIs, not just in design pattern textbooks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Comparator as just a utility interface without seeing it as the canonical Strategy example baked into the standard library
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how lambdas are anonymous strategies and explain why this design lets you sort a list by name, age, or any custom logic without changing the sort method

sections.title: Comparator as Strategy Pattern in Java
sections.content: **Comparator is the textbook Strategy pattern** built into Java's standard library, demonstrating the pattern's power in real production code. The **problem it solves**: you have a list of objects and need to sort them by different criteria — by name, by age, by price, by custom business rules. Without Strategy, you'd need separate sort methods for each criterion or a massive switch statement. **Comparator interface** defines the strategy contract with a compare method that takes two objects and returns negative, zero, or positive integers. Methods like **Collections.sort and List.sort** are the context — they execute the sorting algorithm (quicksort, timsort) but delegate the comparison decision to the injected Comparator. **The brilliance**: the sorting algorithm stays the same, only the comparison logic changes. You can sort the same list by employee name, then by salary, then by hire date, all by passing different Comparator implementations to the same sort method. **Lambda expressions** are anonymous strategy implementations, making the pattern even cleaner. This design is why Java's sorting is so flexible without needing dozens of specialized sort methods.

sections.title: Comparator Strategy Examples
Key Points
content: **Comparator interface**: acts as the strategy interface defining a compare method that returns negative, zero, or positive to indicate ordering relationship between two objects
**List.sort and Collections.sort**: context methods that execute sorting algorithms but delegate element comparison to the injected Comparator strategy, separating algorithm from comparison logic
**Lambda expressions**: are anonymous strategy implementations that let you define comparison logic inline without creating separate classes, making the pattern more concise
**Comparator.comparing factory**: creates strategy instances using method references, enabling fluent API style where you chain comparison criteria with thenComparing
**Strategy composition**: Comparator allows chaining multiple comparison strategies with thenComparing, creating complex sorting rules from simple building blocks
**Runtime strategy selection**: you can decide which Comparator to use based on user input or configuration, passing different strategies to the same sort call without changing the sort method
**Reusable strategies**: concrete Comparator classes like SalaryDescendingComparator can be stored as constants and reused across the application, centralizing comparison logic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Comparator is the perfect example of Strategy pattern that's already in Java. The way it works is List.sort and Collections.sort are the context methods that need to compare elements while sorting, but they don't know how to compare your specific objects. So they take a Comparator as a parameter, which is the strategy interface. When you call list.sort and pass a Comparator, you're injecting a comparison strategy. For example, if you have a list of Employee objects, you can sort them by name by passing a lambda that compares names, or by salary by passing a different lambda. The sort method doesn't change, only the comparison logic changes. That's the core of Strategy pattern. The really cool part is lambdas are anonymous strategies. When you write employees.sort with a lambda comparing Employee name, you're creating a Comparator strategy on the fly without needing a separate class. Java also gives you Comparator.comparing which is a factory that builds strategies using method references, so you can write Comparator.comparing Employee colon colon age and it creates the strategy for you. You can even chain them with thenComparing to sort by age then by salary. The reason this design is so powerful is you can sort the same list ten different ways by passing ten different Comparators, without writing ten different sort methods. Freshers sometimes think Comparator is just an interface for sorting, but it's actually the canonical Strategy example in the Java standard library. Recognizing design patterns in real APIs shows you understand them beyond textbook definitions. The key takeaway is Strategy pattern isn't just an academic concept, it's how Java designed one of its most-used features.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Comparator is Strategy in disguise — and it's been in Java since version 1, making it the most used example of the pattern most developers have never noticed.

beats.content: Collections.sort() is the context — the sorting algorithm is fixed. Comparator is the strategy interface — you inject the comparison rule. Sort by name, sort by salary, sort by date: three strategies, one sort method that never changes.

With Java 8 lambdas, the strategy collapses to one line: list.sort((a, b) -> a.getSalary() - b.getSalary()). A lambda is an anonymous strategy implementation. Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName).thenComparing(Employee::getAge) composes multiple strategies in sequence.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: Almost every functional interface in Java is a strategy — Runnable, Predicate, Function, Callable. Strategy pattern is the foundation of the entire functional programming style Java adopted in version 8.

question: How do you use Spring's @Qualifier annotation for Strategy pattern-style selection?
title: Strategy Pattern with Spring @Qualifier
direct_answer: Annotate each strategy implementation with both at-Component and at-Qualifier with a unique name, then inject the desired strategy using at-Autowired and at-Qualifier in the context class. Spring's dependency injection selects the right bean at startup based on the qualifier name.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how to apply design patterns using Spring's DI container instead of manual instantiation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using new StrategyImpl() inside the context class, which breaks dependency injection and makes testing harder
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the Map injection technique where Spring injects all strategies into a map keyed by qualifier, enabling dynamic runtime selection

sections.title: Spring Qualifier for Strategy Selection
sections.content: **at-Qualifier annotation** solves the problem of multiple beans implementing the same interface in Spring's dependency injection container. Without it, when Spring sees at-Autowired PaymentStrategy in your service and finds three implementations, it throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException because it doesn't know which one to inject. **Qualifier acts as a bean identifier** that tells Spring exactly which implementation you want. You annotate each strategy class with both at-Component and at-Qualifier giving it a unique name, then in the context class you use at-Autowired and at-Qualifier together to request that specific bean. **The power**: you get Strategy pattern benefits — clean separation of algorithms, Open-Closed Principle — plus Spring manages the lifecycle and wiring. **Advanced technique**: inject all strategies into a Map where the key is the qualifier name and the value is the strategy bean. This enables **runtime selection** where you pick the strategy based on user input or configuration, the best of both worlds. Spring's DI container becomes your strategy factory, eliminating the need for manual factory classes and making testing trivial since you can inject mocks.

sections.title: Qualifier-Based Strategy Injection
Key Points
content: **at-Qualifier annotation**: identifies a specific bean when multiple implementations of the same interface exist, preventing Spring's NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup
**at-Component with at-Qualifier**: marks a class as a Spring-managed bean and gives it a unique name that other components can reference during injection
**Constructor injection with at-Qualifier**: use at-Autowired on the constructor (implicit in Spring 4.3+) and at-Qualifier on the parameter to tell Spring which bean to inject
**Compile-time wiring**: using at-Qualifier in the context class constructor locks the strategy choice at compile time, good for fixed configurations where one service always uses one strategy
**Map injection technique**: Spring can inject all beans of an interface type into a Map where keys are qualifier names and values are bean instances, enabling runtime strategy selection
**Runtime strategy selection**: with Map injection, you pass a string parameter that matches a qualifier name and retrieve the corresponding strategy from the map, giving you dynamic behavior
**Testability improvement**: using Spring DI instead of new keyword makes unit testing easy since you can inject mock strategies through the constructor in test classes

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When you have multiple Strategy implementations in Spring, you use at-Qualifier to tell Spring which one to inject. Here's how it works. Each strategy class gets two annotations: at-Component so Spring manages it as a bean, and at-Qualifier with a unique name like email or sms. Then in your context service, you use at-Autowired on the constructor with at-Qualifier on the parameter to say which strategy you want. For example, if you have EmailNotification, SMSNotification, and PushNotification all implementing NotificationStrategy, you'd annotate each with at-Component and at-Qualifier with their respective names. In OrderNotificationService, you'd inject the strategy you want by writing at-Qualifier email in the constructor parameter. Spring sees that and injects the EmailNotification bean. The key thing is you're not using new to create the strategy, Spring handles the instantiation and injection. This makes testing way easier because you can pass mock strategies in your tests. There's also an advanced technique where you inject all strategies into a Map. Spring automatically creates a map where the keys are the qualifier names and the values are the strategy beans. So you'd have a map with entries like email maps to EmailNotification, sms maps to SMSNotification. Then at runtime, you can pick the strategy based on user input by getting it from the map. For example, if the user selects sms as their preferred notification method, you'd do strategies.get sms and get the SMS strategy. This gives you the flexibility of runtime selection without losing the benefits of dependency injection. Freshers often make the mistake of creating strategies with new inside the service, which breaks DI and makes testing harder. Always let Spring inject your strategies.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Spring makes Strategy pattern nearly effortless — the framework wires all implementations into a map automatically.

beats.content: @Qualifier works for fixed selection: annotate CreditCardPaymentStrategy with @Component and @Qualifier('creditCard'), then inject it where you always want that specific implementation. Straightforward and explicit.

Map injection is more powerful for dynamic selection. Annotate all strategies with @Component. Inject Map<String, PaymentStrategy> into the context service — Spring populates the map with every PaymentStrategy bean, using the bean name as the key. At runtime: strategies.get('upiPaymentStrategy'). Adding a new strategy class automatically registers it in the map with no other changes needed.

speakable_v2.cap: gotcha: Bean names in the map use Spring's default naming convention — typically the class name with the first letter lowercased. If the map lookup returns null, check that your key matches the actual bean name, not what you assumed it would be.

question: How is Strategy pattern different from simple polymorphism via inheritance?
title: Strategy Pattern vs Inheritance Polymorphism
direct_answer: Inheritance fixes behavior at compile time by defining it in the class hierarchy, making it hard to swap or combine. Strategy uses composition to inject behavior at runtime, allowing different algorithms to be swapped without changing the context class. Strategy favors flexibility; inheritance favors shared implementation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the fundamental trade-off between inheritance and composition, and when Strategy is the right choice
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying they're the same because both involve polymorphism, missing that Strategy enables runtime swapping while inheritance does not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the composition-over-inheritance principle and show a concrete case where inheritance fails but Strategy succeeds, like needing to change sorting mid-execution

sections.title: Strategy vs Inheritance Polymorphism
sections.content: Both Strategy pattern and inheritance achieve **polymorphism** — the ability to use different implementations through a common interface. But they differ fundamentally in **when behavior is bound** and **how it's composed**. Inheritance polymorphism means you define subclasses like FastShipping extends Shipping and SlowShipping extends Shipping. Each subclass overrides abstract methods. The behavior is **fixed at compile time** — when you create a FastShipping object, it's always fast, forever. You can't change a FastShipping instance into SlowShipping at runtime. Strategy uses **composition instead of inheritance**. Your context class has a field of type Strategy interface and receives the concrete strategy via constructor or setter. The behavior is **bound at runtime** — you can pass a FastShipping strategy, then later replace it with a SlowShipping strategy on the same context instance. Strategy also avoids the **fragile base class problem** — changes to a parent class don't ripple down and break subclasses. The trade-off: inheritance lets subclasses share implementation via protected methods, but Strategy requires each strategy to be fully self-contained. The **Gang of Four's advice** is prefer composition over inheritance — use Strategy when you need **runtime flexibility**, inheritance when you need **shared code reuse**.

sections.title: When to Use Each Approach
sections.content: Use **inheritance polymorphism** when you have a clear is-a relationship and behaviors are **immutable per instance**. For example, if you're modeling vehicles where Car and Truck are fundamentally different types with fixed behavior, inheritance makes sense. Car always has four wheels and a trunk; Truck always has a cargo bed. The behavior won't change at runtime. Use **Strategy pattern** when behavior **varies independently of the object's identity** and needs to be **swappable**. For example, a Document object might need different export strategies: PDF, Word, HTML. A Document is still a Document regardless of export format. You don't want ExportToPDFDocument subclass because the document's identity hasn't changed — only the export algorithm. Strategy also wins when you need to **combine behaviors** — you might have a Logger with different formatting strategies and different destination strategies. With inheritance, you'd need LoggerCSVToFile, LoggerJSONToFile, LoggerCSVToCloud, LoggerJSONToCloud — a combinatorial explosion. With Strategy, you compose two separate strategies at runtime: Formatter strategy and Destination strategy. Finally, if you find yourself writing multiple levels of inheritance just to vary one aspect of behavior, that's a code smell — switch to Strategy. The rule of thumb: inheritance for what something **is**, Strategy for how something **behaves**.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Compile-time vs runtime**: inheritance binds behavior when the object is created, Strategy allows swapping behavior after creation
**Composition over inheritance**: Strategy follows the principle of favoring composition, avoiding tight coupling to class hierarchies
**Single Responsibility**: with Strategy, each algorithm is isolated in its own class, easier to modify without affecting others
**Combinatorial explosion**: inheritance requires subclasses for every combination of features, Strategy composes behaviors independently
**Testability**: Strategy separates concerns — you can mock or stub strategies in tests without complex inheritance hierarchies
**Open-Closed Principle**: Strategy is open for extension (new strategies) and closed for modification (context stays unchanged)
**Polymorphism in both**: both use interfaces or abstract classes, but Strategy adds a layer of indirection via delegation

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Strategy pattern and inheritance polymorphism both let you use different implementations through a common type, but they differ in when behavior is decided and how flexible it is. With inheritance, you create subclasses like FastShipping and SlowShipping that extend a Shipping base class. Each overrides methods like calculateDeliveryTime. The problem is behavior is fixed at compile time — when you create a new FastShipping object, it's always fast. You can't change it to slow later. If you need a different behavior, you have to create a new object of a different class. That's inheritance polymorphism: the behavior is part of the class identity. Strategy pattern uses composition instead. Your ShippingService class has a field of type ShippingStrategy interface, and you inject the concrete strategy via constructor or setter. You can pass a FastShippingStrategy or SlowShippingStrategy, and you can even swap it at runtime by calling setStrategy with a different implementation. That's the key difference: Strategy enables runtime behavior swapping. The object's identity stays the same, but its behavior changes. Here's a concrete example: imagine you're sorting a list. With inheritance, you'd create a SortByName class and SortByAge class, each with its own sort method. But what if you want to sort the same list first by name, then by age? You'd have to process the list twice with different objects. With Strategy, you pass the list to a generic sort method that accepts a Comparator strategy. You call sort with NameComparator, get the result, then call it again with AgeComparator. Same list, same method, different behavior. The trade-off is inheritance lets subclasses share code — the parent class can have protected helper methods that all children use. With Strategy, each strategy class is independent, so if they need shared logic, you have to extract it into a separate utility or use composition there too. The Gang of Four's advice is prefer composition over inheritance, which means prefer Strategy when you need flexibility. Use inheritance when you have a true is-a relationship and behaviors are immutable per object type. The mistake freshers make is thinking they're interchangeable just because both involve polymorphism. They're not — Strategy is specifically for swappable behaviors, inheritance is for shared structure and identity.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Strategy and polymorphism solve the same problem — but one bakes behavior into the class at compile time and the other injects it at runtime.

beats.content: With inheritance polymorphism, the algorithm is tied to the class. A Car subclass overrides calcToll() and that's fixed. If toll rules change on weekends, you'd need to subclass Car again or add conditional logic inside calcToll().

With Strategy, the same Car class holds a TollStrategy reference. You can swap in WeekendTollStrategy at runtime without touching Car. The algorithm changes independently of the object. That's composition over inheritance — the GoF's own recommendation.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: Use inheritance when behavior is intrinsic to type identity — a Dog barks because it IS a Dog. Use Strategy when behavior varies independently of the type — a Car uses different toll rules depending on day and time, not on what kind of car it is.
